questions.question: What is CSS?
options: A stylesheet language that associates rules with HTML elements.
questions.explanation: CSS works by associating rules with HTML elements. Those rules govern how specified elements should be displayed.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant

options: A function and a return type.
A class and an id, always.
A media query and a loop.
questions.explanation: A CSS rule contains two parts: a selector and a declaration.

questions.question: What does the selector do?
options: Indicate which element the rule applies to.
questions.explanation: Selectors indicate which element the rule applies to.

reference.book: HTML and CSS: Design and Build Websites by Jon Duckett

A selector and a media query.
A comment and a semicolon only.

questions.question: Author styles vs user agent styles: who wins by default?
options: Yours (author styles) override the browser defaults.
questions.explanation: Yours are called author styles; user agent styles are the browser's defaults and have lower priority.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: A declaration that “wins” the cascade is called a cascaded value.

questions.question: If two rules have the same specificity, which wins?
options: The one that was written first.
The later one in source order.
questions.explanation: Given the same specificity, later styles override earlier styles.

a:visited { color: purple; }
a:hover { text-decoration: underline; }

questions.question: Which selector is most specific here?
questions.explanation: The most specific selector is the one with one ID, so its declaration is applied.

questions.question: Two classes vs one class plus three tags?
options: Two classes are more specific than one class.
questions.explanation: Selector d has a higher specificity than selector c: two classes are more specific than one class.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: The exact rules of specificity are:  If a selector has more IDs, it wins (that is, it’s more specific).  If that results in a tie, the selector with the most classes wins.  If that results in a tie, the selector with the most tag names wins.

questions.question: What is a cascaded value?
options: At most one winning value per property per element.
questions.explanation: There's at most one cascaded value per property per element. The cascade chooses only one when rendering.

reference.book: CSS in Depth, 1st Edition by Keith J. Grant
reference.excerpt: This is the cascaded value. cascaded value - A value for a particular property applied to an element as a result of the cascade.

questions.question: Can one paragraph have two different top margins from CSS?
options: No. The cascade chooses one top margin.
questions.explanation: A particular paragraph can have a top margin and a bottom margin, but it can't have two different top margins.

questions.question: Why not fix every conflict with !important?
options: It blows a hole in the cascade. Specificity and order stop being tools you can reason about.
questions.explanation: Grant's cascade chapter is how to control which styles apply. !important skips that control.
